title: Learning from Inquests: Families' experiences, limits of PFDs and proposals for a national oversight system
label: 3 November 2026 · Learning from Inquests
summary: Bereaved families, INQUEST and academic experts told the Justice Committee that the current inquest follow-up system fails to learn from deaths. Prevention of future deaths reports (PFDs) are rare, inconsistently used, and not enforced; disclosure and legal support are uneven; and there is no national database to spot trends. Witnesses urged a small independent oversight body (or commissioner) plus a statutory national inquest database and clearer early legal support for families so lessons actually change practice.

glossary.definition: A formal public judicial inquiry held by a coroner to establish who died, and when, where and how.
Prevention of Future Deaths report: a coroner’s recommendation to prevent similar deaths, but without legal enforcement powers.
A judicial officer who investigates sudden, unexplained or state-related deaths and may hold an inquest.
An inquest required where the state may be responsible for a death, demanding a higher level of scrutiny and often a jury.
Care Quality Commission: the regulator for health and social care services in England.
Assessment, Care in Custody and Teamwork: the prison suicide prevention case management process.
A proposed change to allow earlier legal funding for bereaved families in some inquests where public bodies are involved.

chapters.title: Why families came to give evidence
chapters.takeaway: Bereaved families described long, traumatic processes where inquests often failed to produce change, and legal help or data was inconsistent.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We asked families and experts to explain how inquests could better lead to change. Could you briefly introduce yourselves and why you want reform?

turns.speaker: Johnny Santer
turns.text: I run Gabe’s law after my son Gabriel died falling from a multi-storey car park in 2020. The system felt broken: no prevention of future deaths report, delayed disclosure, and I lacked legal support.

turns.speaker: Richard Caseby
turns.text: My son Matthew died after escaping from a privately run psychiatric unit. I investigated, secured legal aid, and fought through an article 2 inquest that showed defensive behaviour from public bodies.

turns.speaker: Dr Szymankiewicz
turns.text: Our daughter Ruth died in an NHS-commissioned private unit; the jury found unlawful killing but the coroner did not issue a PFD. The inquest was retraumatising and we saw little change afterwards.

turns.speaker: Tessa Munt
turns.text: What did you expect an inquest might achieve at the start, and did legal representation make a difference?

turns.speaker: Johnny Santer
turns.text: I knew the four factual questions an inquest answers, but went in without a bundle or representation and left feeling blindsided; seeing other bereaved families with good representation showed how much it helps.

turns.speaker: Richard Caseby
turns.text: I underestimated the process and tried to do it myself before securing specialist lawyers; having legal aid made the difference between being overwhelmed and being able to stand up to large organisations.

turns.speaker: Dr Szymankiewicz
turns.text: We only found INQUEST by chance and then got excellent lawyers who enabled the coroner and jury to consider a wider picture; without them, many questions about Ruth’s care would never have been explored.

chapters.title: Core problems families and experts described
chapters.takeaway: Key failings were late or missing disclosure, an adversarial culture, wide variability between coroners, and PFDs that are rare and not enforceable.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: Richard, only your case among the panel actually had a PFD. How did that feel and what happened next?

turns.speaker: Richard Caseby
turns.text: The PFD highlighted failures like poor records and weak security fences; it led to prosecutions of the Priory and some local changes, but I had to use my own investigative and professional resources to force action.

turns.speaker: Mrs Russell
turns.text: Kate and Johnny, what was the impact of not having a PFD?

turns.speaker: Johnny Santer
turns.text: Without a PFD, Q‑Park faced no regulatory action; six years on there’s still no systemic fix and I had to pursue civil action simply to get basic information.

turns.speaker: Dr Szymankiewicz
turns.text: We were baffled the coroner didn’t issue a PFD given the jury’s unlawful killing verdict and systemic list of failures. Even when PFDs exist, families often don’t see meaningful change.

turns.speaker: Warinder Juss
turns.text: Are there other problems in the follow-up approach we should note?

turns.speaker: Johnny Santer
turns.text: PFDs cover only a tiny slice of inquests; most learning opportunities are missed because PFDs are the narrow focus and many similar deaths get no system-wide attention.

turns.speaker: Richard Caseby
turns.text: There’s huge variability between coroners: some are rigorous, some aren’t; and public bodies turn up with legal teams defending reputations, not helping find solutions.

turns.speaker: Dr Szymankiewicz
turns.text: Coronial practice varies and often relies on providers’ own records; families need independent evidence-gathering in complex settings such as mental health units.

turns.speaker: Dr Shastri-Hurst
turns.text: Late disclosure was mentioned—does that happen only to litigants in person or more widely?

turns.speaker: Deborah Coles
turns.text: Late disclosure happens whether families are represented or not. Early legal representation can protect families and improve pre-inquest investigations, but many families don’t get it.

chapters.title: What the data shows and current transparency problems
chapters.takeaway: PFDs are few and responses have improved but remain inconsistent; there is no national inquest database to spot trends or evaluate policy, and recent administrative changes risk reducing transparency.

turns.speaker: Dr Richards
turns.text: PFDs cover about 1.7% of inquests. We track every PFD since 2013; responses rose from under a third to about two thirds after public tracking, but PFDs alone do not show the full picture.

turns.speaker: Tony Vaughan
turns.text: Has there been progress since the 2021 Justice Committee report?

turns.speaker: Dr Richards
turns.text: Response rates improved, but recent Office of the Chief Coroner changes delay PFD publication until responses arrive and introduced confusing templates—this hinders transparency and rapid learning.

turns.speaker: Deborah Coles
turns.text: We see better recognition by some coroners of linked PFDs, but responses are often formulaic and untested. Families rarely see follow-up verification that promised changes actually happened.

turns.speaker: Mrs Russell
turns.text: Other countries have national coronial databases. What difference would that make here?

turns.speaker: Dr Richards
turns.text: A statutory national inquest database enables real-time alerts, trend analysis and evaluation of policy changes. It already exists in Australia, Canada and other places and is feasible here.

turns.speaker: Deborah Coles
turns.text: Without a central system, systemic failures repeat. High-profile laws like Awaab’s or Seni’s came after campaigning; most families can’t force that change without a national mechanism.

turns.speaker: Dr Richards
turns.text: One stark fact: the Ministry of Justice has historically responded to only about 30% of PFDs—there’s scope for Select Committees, especially Justice, to demand better practice.

chapters.title: Proposals: oversight body, national database and early legal help
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses recommended an independent national oversight mechanism plus a statutory inquest database, powers to follow up PFDs and earlier legal support for families.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Which organisation should monitor and follow up on inquest outcomes?

turns.speaker: Deborah Coles
turns.text: INQUEST proposes a National Oversight Mechanism (NOM): an independent public body that collates recommendations from inquests and inquiries, analyses themes, and follows up implementation with powers to access information.

turns.speaker: Richard Caseby
turns.text: My ideal is a commissioner for prevention of future deaths—a high-profile independent figure with a small secretariat to spot trends, hold organisations to account and report to Parliament.

turns.speaker: Dr Richards
turns.text: Any NOM must be paired with a statutory national database of all inquests so you can identify trends beyond the 1.7% that get PFDs; the tracker already shows how digital dashboards and alerts can work in real time.

turns.speaker: Warinder Juss
turns.text: What powers should that oversight body have—especially where no PFD was issued?

turns.speaker: Deborah Coles
turns.text: It should have the power to request information, escalate repeat risks to regulators or prosecutors, produce public thematic reports for Parliament, and include bereaved people in governance.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: How would it act where there was no PFD but a narrative or jury conclusion showing systemic failure?

turns.speaker: Deborah Coles
turns.text: The NOM would collate inquest conclusions, not just PFDs, so jury findings and other recommendations feed into national learning and trigger follow-up when patterns appear.

turns.speaker: Dr Richards
turns.text: Digital infrastructure matters: standardised templates, a statutory data flow from coroners to the NOM, and live public dashboards so Parliament and regulators can act quickly.

turns.speaker: Tony Vaughan
turns.text: Could existing bodies do this, or does it need a new organisation?

turns.speaker: Richard Caseby
turns.text: Existing bodies like the NAO don't fit well; you need an independent, focused body with moral authority to press change across Departments and report into Parliamentary oversight.

turns.speaker: Deborah Coles
turns.text: A new, properly resourced body is needed—one that can bring cross-government accountability and be independent from the institutions it will scrutinise.

turns.speaker: Janet Daby
turns.text: If you had one message for Government, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Dr Szymankiewicz
turns.text: Put bereaved families at the centre, create an oversight mechanism that actually changes practice, and bring Ministers from all Departments together to act on repeated failures.

turns.speaker: Johnny Santer
turns.text: We want lessons to be learned so other families do not suffer the same avoidable losses—end the cliff edge after PFDs: follow-up must be real and visible.

turns.speaker: Richard Caseby
turns.text: Appoint a commissioner, build a national database and stop the mantra that 'lessons will be learned' when they rarely are—give the oversight body powers to spotlight repeated failings.

chapters.title: Closing: practical steps and next actions
chapters.takeaway: Families and experts asked the Committee to press for a statutory inquest database, an independent oversight body with follow-up powers, and earlier funded legal support for families.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. We will press the evidence: fund and establish a national inquest database, consider a National Oversight Mechanism, and look at early legal funding triggers like Hillsborough law.

turns.speaker: Deborah Coles
turns.text: Please make the oversight body's first role to ensure families actually see what has happened to recommendations—transparency and follow-up are the essentials.

turns.speaker: Dr Richards
turns.text: Fund the digital work: the tracker shows what’s possible now—real-time alerts, analysis and public dashboards would transform learning from deaths.

turns.speaker: Johnny Santer
turns.text: Act now so Gabe and others did not die in vain. Families cannot forever be the ones who must expose and fix systemic risk.

turns.speaker: Richard Caseby
turns.text: End the cliff edge of PFDs: appoint someone to follow up, spot trends and hold organisations to account.

turns.speaker: Dr Szymankiewicz
turns.text: Make sure reforms directly reduce the day-to-day risks that killed our loved ones—start with mental health units and children’s access to family.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you to all witnesses and families for their courage and clarity today; your evidence will shape our recommendations.
